subject: Physics and Chemistry
scope: Forty existing original short school-mock flashcards, 20 Physics AS and 20 Chemistry AS/taught A2, across waves, mechanics, particles, electricity, quantities, bonding, Kp, entropy and optical isomerism. Does not add flashcards.
method: Exact ID, prompt, model answer, subject, mock eligibility and stage guards only. Preserve earlier accepted and rejected examples; newly approved full correct paraphrases and false misconceptions are checked against production evaluateCard using an exact-list override before fuzzy scoring.
limitations: This review tests forty specifically sourced cards, not all AQA specification bullets.
Unseen written answers may not be correctly classified; longer proof, mechanism, diagram and calculation methods need separate review.
XP, school-mock filter, question texts, existing flashcard text, cloud sync and saved progress must remain unchanged.

accept: Impulse is the triangle area: half of 0.20 seconds times 80 newtons, or 8.0 N s.
reject: Impulse is 80 N s because the peak force is the area.
Impulse is 16 N s because it is always a rectangle.
rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Force rises 0→80 N then returns to 0 over 0.20 s. Find impulse.
rows.originalBack: Area of triangular F–t graph = ½×0.20×80 = 8.0 N s (change in momentum).

accept: Impulse means change in momentum, and equals FΔt for a constant resultant force.
reject: Impulse is defined as the change in kinetic energy.
Impulse equals mass multiplied by displacement.
rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is an impulse?
rows.originalBack: Change in momentum, FΔt.

accept: Tensile strain is ΔL divided by the original length L, with no unit.
reject: Tensile strain is F/A and is measured in pascals.
Tensile strain is measured in newtons per metre.
rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is tensile strain?
rows.originalBack: strain = ΔL/L; it has no unit.

accept: Tensile stress is force divided by cross-sectional area, F/A, in pascals.
reject: Stress is the extension divided by initial length and has no units.
Stress is force multiplied by area and measured in N m².
rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is tensile stress?
rows.originalBack: stress = F/A, in Pa.

accept: A wavelength is the least distance between two points oscillating in phase.
reject: Wavelength is the spacing between the next crest and trough.
Wavelength is the maximum displacement from equilibrium.
rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is wavelength?
rows.originalBack: Shortest distance between two points in phase.

accept: Half a period corresponds to 180 degrees or pi radians of phase difference.
reject: Half a cycle is 360 degrees or two pi radians.
Half a cycle is 90 degrees or pi over two radians.
rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What phase difference is half a cycle?
rows.originalBack: π radians or 180°.

accept: For the fundamental vibration on a fixed string its length holds half a wavelength, so λ=2L.
reject: The fundamental string wavelength is L/2.
One entire wavelength fits into the string length for the first harmonic.
rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: For a string fixed at both ends, what is the first-harmonic wavelength?
rows.originalBack: Twice the vibrating length, λ = 2L.

accept: Fringe spacing is the distance between adjacent bright fringes, or between adjacent dark fringes.
reject: Fringe spacing is the distance between one bright fringe and its neighbouring dark fringe.
Fringe spacing is the physical separation of the slits.
rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is fringe spacing?
rows.originalBack: Distance between adjacent bright fringes or adjacent dark fringes.

accept: At unchanged wavelength and screen distance, wider slit separation produces narrower fringes.
reject: Increasing double-slit separation makes fringe spacing increase.
Changing slit separation has no effect on fringe spacing.
rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What happens to fringe spacing if the double-slit separation increases?
rows.originalBack: It decreases.

accept: At unchanged wavelength and slit separation, moving the screen farther away increases fringe spacing.
reject: Increasing screen distance makes double-slit fringes closer.
Screen distance and fringe separation are unrelated.
rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What happens to fringe spacing if the screen distance increases?
rows.originalBack: It increases.

accept: Stationary waves result from superposition of two coherent waves moving in opposite directions.
reject: Two same-direction waves alone always produce a stationary wave.
A stationary wave requires no superposition of waves.
rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: How do stationary waves form?
rows.originalBack: Two coherent waves travel in opposite directions and superpose.

accept: Neighbouring nodes in a standing wave are half a wavelength apart.
reject: Adjacent nodes are separated by a full wavelength.
Adjacent nodes are separated by one quarter wavelength.
rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: How far apart are adjacent stationary-wave nodes?
rows.originalBack: Half a wavelength, λ/2.

accept: A string's first harmonic frequency depends on its vibrating length, tension and mass per unit length.
reject: Its fundamental frequency depends only on the amplitude.
Tension and linear mass density do not affect a string's fundamental frequency.
rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: In string-wave RP1, what controls the fundamental frequency?
rows.originalBack: Vibrating length, tension and mass per unit length.

accept: When length and linear mass density are fixed, frequency squared is proportional to tension, giving a straight-line graph.
reject: Frequency squared is inversely proportional to tension at constant string length.
Plotting f² against tension always produces a horizontal line at constant density.
rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What relation can be tested by plotting f² against tension?
rows.originalBack: A straight line at fixed length and mass per unit length.

accept: A photon can give its energy to a single electron immediately when its frequency exceeds the threshold.
reject: The electron must accumulate energy slowly from many subthreshold photons.
There is always a substantial delay before emission above the threshold frequency.
rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Why is photoelectric emission effectively immediate above threshold?
rows.originalBack: One photon transfers its energy to one electron in one interaction.

accept: The gradient of a plot of maximum photoelectron kinetic energy against frequency equals Planck's constant h.
reject: The gradient equals the metal work function φ.
The maximum KE versus frequency gradient is the electron charge e.
rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is the gradient of a graph of maximum photoelectron KE against frequency?
rows.originalBack: Planck constant, h.

accept: Antiparticles have equal rest mass and rest energy but opposite electric charge and other additive quantum numbers.
reject: An antiparticle must have less mass than its corresponding particle.
A particle and its antiparticle have identical electric charge and all additive quantum numbers.
rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: How does an antiparticle compare with its particle?
rows.originalBack: Same mass and rest energy, but opposite charge and other additive quantum numbers.

accept: A baryon has three quarks, whereas a meson has a quark and an antiquark.
reject: Baryons contain only two quarks and mesons contain three.
Mesons contain three quarks while baryons contain a quark–antiquark pair.
rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: How do baryons and mesons differ?
rows.originalBack: Baryons contain three quarks; mesons contain a quark and an antiquark.

accept: Power in a resistor can be calculated by P=VI, P=I²R or P=V²/R.
reject: Electrical power is P=V/I in watts.
Electrical power is P=IR² rather than I²R.
rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Give three electrical power equations.
rows.originalBack: P = VI = I²R = V²/R.

accept: Electron momentum p and wavelength λ obey λ=h/p.
reject: Electron de Broglie wavelength equals λ=hp.
Electron wavelength is calculated using λ=p/h instead of h/p.
rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Which equation links an electron's de Broglie wavelength λ with its momentum p?
rows.originalBack: λ = h/p.

accept: In TOF, ionisation charges the sample particles so electric fields can accelerate them and the detector can register them.
reject: Ionisation neutralises all particles so no electric field acts on them.
Ionisation prevents ion detection by removing every charge.
rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is the purpose of ionisation in TOF?
rows.originalBack: To give sample particles an electrical charge so they can be accelerated and detected.

accept: Empirical formula means simplest whole-number atomic ratio; molecular formula gives the actual number of each atom in one molecule.
reject: The empirical formula gives exact molecular atom counts, while molecular formula is the simplest ratio.
Every empirical formula must be identical to the corresponding molecular formula.
rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is the difference between empirical and molecular formula?
rows.originalBack: Empirical: simplest atom ratio. Molecular: actual atoms per molecule.

accept: Assume the composition is from 100 g, so each percentage becomes grams before converting masses to moles.
reject: Treat percentage composition numbers directly as mole values without using atomic mass.
A 25% composition means 25 kg of that element in a 100 g hypothetical sample.
rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: How should percentages be treated when calculating empirical formula?
rows.originalBack: Assume a 100 g sample; percentage values become gram masses.

accept: Divide each element's mass by its Ar, divide the mole amounts by the smallest, then write the whole-number ratio.
reject: Divide each mass by the highest mass and call it an empirical ratio without calculating moles.
Add all the atomic masses instead of finding a mole ratio.
rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What are the three stages of empirical formula calculation?
rows.originalBack: Divide element masses by Ar; divide moles by smallest; find integer ratio.

accept: Find the empirical formula Mr, then calculate molecular Mr divided by it and multiply all empirical subscripts by that factor.
reject: Multiply empirical Mr by molecular Mr to obtain the molecular formula directly.
Divide the empirical subscripts by molecular Mr to obtain the molecular formula.
rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: How is molecular formula calculated from empirical formula?
rows.originalBack: Find empirical-formula Mr, divide molecular Mr by it, multiply subscripts.

accept: First find moles by n=pV/RT using SI units; then calculate molar mass from M=m/n.
reject: Gas molar mass equals moles divided by mass, n/m.
Gas molar mass is M=m×n, not mass divided by moles.
rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: How do you calculate molar mass of an unknown gas from mass and gas data?
rows.originalBack: First n=pV/(RT), then molar mass M=m/n.

accept: In diamond every carbon is covalently bonded to four neighbours in a tetrahedral giant structure.
reject: Each diamond carbon forms three bonds, leaving a mobile electron.
Every carbon in diamond forms two bonds along a linear chain.
rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: How many covalent bonds does each carbon make in diamond?
rows.originalBack: Four, in a three-dimensional tetrahedral network.

accept: Diamond's high melting point is due to strong covalent C–C bonds throughout a giant lattice that require much energy to break.
reject: Diamond melts at a high temperature only due to weak forces between small diamond molecules.
Hydrogen bonds between diamond molecules are the main cause of its high melting point.
rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why does diamond have an extremely high melting point?
rows.originalBack: Many strong covalent C–C bonds throughout the giant lattice must be broken.

accept: There are no delocalised electrons or mobile ions in diamond, so it cannot conduct electricity.
reject: Diamond conducts because each carbon leaves a freely moving electron.
Diamond's lattice contains free positive ions that carry electric current.
rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why does diamond not conduct electricity?
rows.originalBack: No mobile ions or delocalised electrons are available.

accept: Graphite contains hexagonal layers with each carbon bonded to three others and one electron per carbon delocalised.
reject: Each graphite carbon forms four covalent bonds and has no delocalised electrons.
Graphite is made of separate C₂ molecules instead of giant covalent layers.
rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What does graphite's bonding look like?
rows.originalBack: Each C forms three covalent bonds in layers of hexagonal rings; one electron is delocalised.

accept: Delocalised electrons move along graphite's layers, allowing electrical conduction.
reject: Graphite conducts because carbon ions flow freely through its layers.
Graphite cannot conduct because every electron is fixed in a covalent bond.
rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why can graphite conduct along its layers?
rows.originalBack: Delocalised electrons move through the layers.

accept: Outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and more shielded down Group 2, reducing attraction and first ionisation energy.
reject: First ionisation energy rises down Group 2 because the outer electron moves closer to the nucleus.
Ionisation energy falls because nuclear charge gets smaller down Group 2.
rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why does first IE fall down Group 2?
rows.originalBack: Outer electrons are farther away and more shielded, despite a larger nuclear charge.

accept: Changing total pressure at fixed temperature does not change Kp, although the gas equilibrium position may shift.
reject: Increasing total pressure always increases Kp, even without a temperature change.
The equilibrium constant Kp must decrease if total pressure is raised at fixed temperature.
rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Does changing total pressure at constant temperature change Kp?
rows.originalBack: No. It may change equilibrium position, but Kp itself is unchanged at fixed temperature.

accept: Entropy tends to increase as particles become more dispersed, particularly when more gas molecules form.
reject: Making more gaseous particles always decreases the entropy.
A more dispersed arrangement always has lower entropy.
rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: When does entropy usually increase?
rows.originalBack: When particles become more dispersed/disordered, especially when more gas particles are formed.

accept: Catalysts lower activation energy and can increase reaction rate, but they do not alter ΔG or thermodynamic feasibility.
reject: A catalyst makes the standard Gibbs energy more negative and changes thermodynamic feasibility.
Catalysts cannot increase rate but always change the overall ΔG.
rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Does a catalyst change ΔG or thermodynamic feasibility?
rows.originalBack: No. A catalyst lowers activation energy and increases rate; it does not change ΔG for the overall reaction.

accept: A carbon bonded to four different groups may produce enantiomers, which are mirror images that cannot be superimposed.
reject: Any two compounds with the same molecular formula must be optical isomers.
Enantiomers have mirror-image structures that can be perfectly superimposed.
rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What causes optical isomerism?
rows.originalBack: A chiral carbon bonded to four different groups gives non-superimposable mirror-image enantiomers.

accept: A ketone has a carbonyl group whose carbon atom is bonded to two carbon-containing groups.
reject: A ketone carbonyl has a hydrogen directly attached to its carbon, as in an aldehyde.
The ketone group is simply an alcohol's OH group with no C=O.
rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is the functional group in a ketone?
rows.originalBack: Carbonyl group between two carbon atoms.

accept: Attack on either face of a planar C=O may give different configurations and enantiomers when a chiral centre is formed.
reject: A planar carbonyl can be attacked from only one side so enantiomers never form.
Attack from either face of a carbonyl must give the same superimposable product even when chirality develops.
rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why can some carbonyl additions create enantiomer pairs?
rows.originalBack: Attack from opposite faces of the planar carbonyl creates different configurations.

accept: Two readings each with an uncertainty of 0.1°C give a maximum ΔT uncertainty of 0.2°C by addition.
reject: The uncertainty in a temperature difference is zero when using the same thermometer.
The uncertainty becomes 0.01°C because the two reading uncertainties are multiplied.
rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: A thermometer is ±0.1°C per reading. What is the uncertainty in ΔT?
rows.originalBack: ±0.2°C: add the absolute uncertainties of initial and final readings.

accept: The acyl chloride functional group is –COCl, a carbonyl carbon bonded directly to chlorine.
reject: Acyl chloride contains –COOH rather than –COCl.
The defining acyl chloride group is –NH₂ with no carbonyl group.
rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What does an acyl chloride contain?
rows.originalBack: The –COCl functional group.
